title: Mercury acquire five-time All-Star Plum; Sparks signal formal rebuild after contention failure
dek: The Phoenix Mercury acquired five-time All-Star Kelsey Plum from the Los Angeles Sparks in exchange for Monique Akoa Makani, a 2027 first-round pick, and a 2028 second-rounder. The trade marks the fourth All-Star midseason trade in WNBA history and the Sparks' formal abandonment of their failed contention experiment.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: The Mercury sent Monique Akoa Makani, a 2027 first-rounder, and a 2028 second-rounder to acquire five-time All-Star Kelsey Plum from the Sparks.
bottom_line: The Mercury are betting assets on Plum's scoring prowess to salvage a playoff run, while the Sparks have formally reset with new interim leadership and are accepting a rebuild. Watch for Plum's return timeline and early performance with the Mercury, and whether the Sparks' management transition leads to measurable strategic clarity.
body: The Phoenix Mercury acquired five-time All-Star Kelsey Plum from the Los Angeles Sparks on Saturday night, sending Monique Akoa Makani, a 2027 first-round pick, and a 2028 second-rounder in return. The deal closed late Saturday with the WNBA trade deadline set for Sunday afternoon, marking just the fourth time in league history that an All-Star has been traded midseason.

Plum is a two-time WNBA champion currently averaging 23.9 points and 6.4 assists through 12 games, both career highs. Earlier this season, she led the WNBA in scoring before being sidelined by a lower left leg injury on June 21. The Mercury's timeline for her availability is unclear, though she had been expected to return for the Sparks' Sunday game at Portland. It is unknown whether she will play when the Mercury face Chicago on Monday.

The Mercury entered the trade at 11-19, 13 games out of first place and six games behind the eighth-place New York Liberty. They reached the WNBA Finals last season. The addition of Plum at scoring volume represents a high-stakes bet on a playoff push in the season's final stretch.

Plum has also missed time earlier this season with an ankle injury. Per ESPN reporting, she intends to pursue full free agency in the offseason, meaning the Mercury's asset investment may not result in long-term retention despite the multiple picks surrendered.

The Sparks, meanwhile, are 10-17 and mired in a six-game losing streak, posting a 2-9 record without Plum. The trade formalizes the organization's pivot away from its failed contention experiment. Earlier this month, the Sparks parted ways with general manager Raegan Pebley and elevated assistant general managers Zach Knowlton and Nate Nielsen, both new to the WNBA, in an interim capacity. The team remains unlikely to make the playoffs for a sixth consecutive season.

The Sparks' trajectory illustrates a pattern of strategic missteps. After initially committing to a rebuild and drafting Cameron Brink and Rickea Jackson in 2024, the organization traded away the No. 2 draft pick ahead of the 2025 campaign to acquire Plum. In the offseason, they brought in veterans Nneka Ogwumike and Ariel Atkins, trading Jackson to acquire the latter. That investment has not yielded results. CBS Sports labeled the Mercury's move a "head-scratching" acquisition, suggesting skepticism about the asset cost for an injured player headed toward free agency.
